Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Sterling Bank Group Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, ladies and gentlemen, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to review Sterling Bank Group's results for the Q3 2024. With me this morning are John Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer; and Lisa Patel, Chief Risk Officer.

Before we begin, let me remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of these factors.

I will now turn the call over to John Reynolds.

John Reynolds:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Sterling Bank Group delivered solid performance in the Q3 2024, demonstrating the strength of our diversified business model and our commitment to serving our customers.

Our key priorities for this year remain focused on:
1. Enhancing customer experience
2. Driving operational efficiency
3. Investing in strategic growth initiatives
4. Maintaining strong capital levels.

Now, I'd like to provide some highlights on the macroeconomic outlook and its impact on our business, trends in our operating expenses, our technology investments and their efficiency gains, and our reserve build and release dynamics. Our diversified franchise across retail banking, commercial lending, wealth management, and capital markets continues to position us well. I'll touch on the high-level points here, and Michael will provide more color shortly.

The macroeconomic environment shows resilience with some bifurcation, supporting our net interest margin expansion and disciplined lending. We've managed expenses tightly while investing in tech to boost productivity. And our credit reserves reflect prudent management with strong coverage. Overall, these elements underscore our resilient growth strategy.

I will now turn the call over to Michael Chen to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Michael Chen:
Thank you, John, and good morning, everyone. Sterling Bank Group reported net income of $850 million for the Q3 2024, or $1.45 per share. Our results reflect strong revenue growth, disciplined expense management, and a healthy credit environment.

Net interest income increased 8% year-over-year driven by higher interest rates and loan growth. Non-interest income was impacted by lower trading revenues. We continue to maintain a strong capital position with a CET1 ratio of 12.8%. 

As we review our Q3 results, I'd like to spend a few minutes on the macroeconomic environment and its implications for Sterling Bank Group. Our diversified franchise across retail banking, commercial lending, wealth management, and capital markets positions us well to navigate the current landscape.

Starting with the global macro picture: We're seeing a resilient yet bifurcated recovery. The IMF's latest World Economic Outlook projects global GDP growth at 3.1% for 2024, down slightly from 3.2% last year, with advanced economies at 1.7% and emerging markets accelerating to 4.2%. Inflation has broadly cooled—global CPI now hovering around 5.8% year-over-year—but persistent services inflation and supply chain frictions remain headwinds. Geopolitical risks, including the ongoing Middle East tensions and U.S.-China trade frictions, have pushed the VIX to an average of 18 in Q3, up 15% quarter-over-quarter, contributing to market volatility.

In the U.S., our core market representing 65% of our loan book, the soft landing narrative holds firm. Fed funds remain at 5.25-5.50%, with the September dot plot signaling 50 bps of cuts by year-end and another 100 bps in 2025. Core PCE inflation eased to 2.7% in August, while unemployment ticked up to 4.1%. Consumer spending grew 2.8% annualized in Q3, supported by real wage gains of 1.2%, but delinquencies on credit cards have risen to 3.2%—the highest since 2011—signaling some stretch in lower FICO segments. For us, this has driven NIM expansion to 3.45% in Q3, up 12 basis points quarter-over-quarter, as our deposit beta lagged at 65% during the rate hike cycle. Loan demand remains tepid at 4.2% YoY growth, concentrated in C&I and CRE, where we’ve tightened underwriting on office exposure to 15% of our portfolio, down from 18% a year ago.

Commercial real estate merits a deeper dive: Multifamily and industrial segments are resilient, with cap rates stabilizing at 5.2-6.0%, but office vacancy rates hit 19.5% nationally. We've de-risked proactively—our CRE criticized loans are at just 2.8% of total CRE, versus the industry average of 5.1% per FDIC data—and our CET1 ratio stands at a rock-solid 12.8%, well above Basel III endgame requirements. This discipline has kept our net charge-off rate at 45 bps, 10 bps below peers.

Turning regionally: In Europe, which accounts for 20% of our international operations via our London and Frankfurt hubs, growth is sluggish at 0.9% for the Eurozone per ECB forecasts. The deposit flight to money market funds persists, with €450 billion shifting YTD, pressuring peers' liquidity coverage ratios. Our European NIM compressed to 2.1% but we're offsetting via fee income growth of 8% YoY from trade finance and ESG-linked bonds. We've launched a €2 billion green lending facility mirroring the EU's Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation, targeting renewables and capturing 15% market share in solar project finance.

Asia-Pacific, 10% of our footprint through our Singapore and Mumbai offices, shows divergence: India's GDP is roaring at 6.8%, fueling 12% loan growth in our SME book via UPI-integrated digital lending platforms. Conversely, China's property woes—Evergrande-style defaults lingering—have slowed regional growth to 4.6%, with our exposure limited to 3% of total loans, hedged via cross-currency swaps. We're expanding embedded finance partnerships, akin to what JPMorgan Chase is doing with Walmart, embedding our BNPL product into Indian e-commerce giants like Flipkart, projecting 25% revenue uplift in FY25.

On trends shaping banking: Digital adoption accelerates—global open banking transactions up 40% YoY per Finextra data—with 68% of our retail customers now active on our mobile app. We've invested $250 million in GenAI initiatives, including a proprietary credit risk model using transformer-based NLP on alternative data sources like utility payments and social mobility indices. This has improved PD calibration by 18%, reducing NPL formation by 22 bps in our auto loan portfolio. We're also ahead on ISO 20022 adoption for cross-border payments, processing 1.2 million messages daily with 99.9% straight-through processing.

Strategically, we're positioning for the rate-cutting cycle. Expect loan growth of 5-7% in FY25, NIM stabilizing at 3.4-3.5%, and ROE expanding to 13.5% from 12.8% this year. We're allocating $1.5 billion to buybacks at current valuations—trading at 11.5x forward earnings, a 20% discount to tangible book—and pursuing M&A in fintech adjacencies, like our recent tuck-in of a U.K. regtech firm for real-time AML screening.

Risks? A harder landing with U.S. unemployment breaching 4.5% could pressure consumer loans, where we hold 28% market share in auto originations. We've stress-tested to a 200 bps recession scenario, with PCLs at 120 bps and still generating 10% ROE. On the upside, fiscal stimulus in election-year U.S. and India's capex boom could surprise positively.

In summary on the macro, the backdrop favors incumbents like Sterling with fortress balance sheets and tech-forward strategies. We're executing on our "Resilient Growth 2027" plan—delivering mid-teens EPS CAGR through cycle.

Now, turning to our operating expenses for the third quarter, where we saw continued progress in our multi-year efficiency program, offset by targeted investments in strategic growth areas. Overall, adjusted operating expenses came in at $2.85 billion for the quarter, up 4.2% year-over-year and 1.8% quarter-over-quarter. Excluding a one-time $150 million charge related to our legacy mortgage servicing rights remediation—aligned with FHFA guidelines—this represents a more modest 2.8% YoY increase, in line with our guided range of 3-5% for the full year.

We remain laser-focused on our core efficiency ratio, which improved to 57.8% this quarter from 60.2% a year ago and 58.9% in Q2. This marks our best quarterly reading since the pre-pandemic levels of 2019, driven by revenue growth outpacing expense expansion and proactive cost levers. For context, our peers in the super-regional banking space—like KeyCorp and Regions Financial—have seen efficiency ratios hovering around 60-62% amid similar pressures, so we're gaining share on productivity.

Personnel expenses, which accounted for 52% of total op ex at $1.48 billion, up 3.1% YoY. This reflects a 2.5% merit increase cycle for our 45,000-strong workforce, tempered by a 4% headcount reduction through attrition and selective hiring freezes in non-client-facing back-office roles. We added 250 net new relationship managers in our Commercial Banking segment to capitalize on M&A advisory demand, but offset this with 1,100 reductions in operations via RPA—robotic process automation—deployments. Comp ratio remains competitive at 85% of market median per Equilar data, with deferred comp tied 40% to TSR—total shareholder return—outperformance.

Technology and data expenses, our second-largest line at 22% of op ex or $627 million, rose 12% YoY—the highest growth rate—reflecting our $1.2 billion annual tech budget, up from $950 million in 2022. Key here is our cloud-first migration: 65% of our core workloads are now on AWS and Azure, ahead of our 70% target by year-end, yielding $45 million in annualized run-rate savings from mainframe decommissioning. We're also ramping AI investments, including a $75 million pilot with Palantir for real-time fraud detection in our payments platform, which processed 1.2 billion transactions this quarter with a 15% reduction in false positives versus legacy rules-based systems. Cybersecurity spend ticked up 18% to $120 million, bolstered by post-SVB learnings and enhanced liquidity stress testing under the new Fed tailoring framework.

Occupancy and equipment costs held flat at $285 million, benefiting from our hybrid work model—now 60/40 office/remote—and sublease income from 20% excess space in legacy branches. Professional fees and outside services climbed 8% to $210 million, driven by elevated legal costs from a resolved $50 million class-action on overdraft practices, similar to Wells Fargo's settlements, and consulting for Basel IV implementation, where we're advancing our IRRBB—interest rate risk in the banking book—modeling to comply with EBA standards ahead of 2025.

Regulatory and compliance expenses, at $195 million or 7% of op ex, were up 6% YoY due to ongoing Dodd-Frank stress testing enhancements and deposit insurance premiums, which rose with our $450 billion insured deposit base amid the banking mini-crisis last March. Marketing and business development dipped 2% to $112 million as we shifted to digital channels, with 70% of customer acquisition now via our mobile app and partnerships like Plaid for open banking APIs.

From a macroeconomic standpoint, inflationary pressures—core PCE at 2.6%—continue to embed in vendor contracts and wage growth, but we've contained this through 85% fixed-price multi-year deals with key suppliers like FIS and Fiserv for core processing. Higher interest rates have also juiced funding costs indirectly via talent competition; we're paying 10-15% premiums for quants in our Treasury team to manage our $200 billion securities portfolio amid YCC unwind risks.

Strategically, our "Fit for Growth" initiative—launched in Q4 2022—delivered $320 million in run-rate savings this year, including $180 million from procure-to-pay digitization with Coupa and $140 million from endpoint management consolidation post our Citrix-to-VMware shift. We're targeting another $250 million in 2025 via gen AI for customer service, piloting with Google's Vertex AI to handle 30% of Tier 1 inquiries, potentially cutting call center costs by 20%. This positions us ahead of Big Tech disruptors like Chime or SoFi, who boast sub-50% efficiency ratios but lack our scale in C&I lending.

Regionally, North America drove 75% of op ex growth, with elevated tech spend in our U.S. Consumer Banking unit amid BNPL—buy now, pay later—expansion via Affirm partnerships. Europe, 15% of the total, saw 7% YoY expense growth due to PSD3 compliance investments and Brexit-related dual-stack operations in London and Dublin; however, our efficiency ratio there improved to 55% on strong IB fees. In Asia-Pacific, representing 8% of op ex, costs rose 5% on hiring for wealth management in Singapore and India, where AUM grew 22% to $150 billion, fueled by UHNW migration trends. Emerging markets like LatAm, 2% of total, benefited from shared services offshoring to Bogotá, saving 15% versus U.S. onshore equivalents.

Looking ahead, we expect full-year op ex growth of 3.5-4.5%, with Q4 skewed higher by $80 million in seasonal comp true-ups and variable incentive funding tied to our 12% ROE achievement. Our long-term aspiration remains a 55% efficiency ratio by 2026, supported by 5-7% CAGR in revenue from embedded finance and capital-light fee streams like cards and payments, where interchange revenue hit $450 million this quarter.

I'd like to dive deeper into one of our key strategic pillars: our technology investments and their transformative impact on operational efficiency. In FY2024, we allocated $2.8 billion to technology and digital transformation initiatives—representing 12% of our total operating expenses and a 15% increase year-over-year. This disciplined investment, focused on high-ROI areas like cloud infrastructure, AI-driven automation, and data analytics, has delivered tangible results: our efficiency ratio improved to 52.3% from 58.1% in FY2023, outpacing the industry average of 56% as reported by S&P Global.

First, cloud migration and infrastructure modernization. We've completed 85% of our core banking systems migration to a hybrid multi-cloud environment, leveraging AWS for high-volume transaction processing and Azure for AI workloads. This has reduced our total cost of ownership by 28% on migrated workloads, primarily through elastic scaling and eliminating legacy mainframe depreciation costs, which previously accounted for $450 million annually. Processing times for real-time payments via our RTP-enabled platform have dropped from 15 seconds to under 2 seconds, boosting straight-through processing rates to 98.5%—a level competitive with JPMorgan Chase's own cloud-native capabilities.

Second, AI and machine learning applications. Our $650 million investment in genAI and ML has been a game-changer. In fraud detection, our proprietary ML models—integrated with graph analytics similar to those used by FIS and Temenos—flagged 1.2 million anomalous transactions last year, reducing fraud losses by 42% to $185 million, or just 4 basis points of total assets. On the customer-facing side, our AI-powered virtual assistant, built on Google Cloud's Vertex AI and handling 65% of Tier 1 inquiries, has cut call center volumes by 32%, saving $120 million in FTE costs while achieving a 92% first-contact resolution rate. This mirrors trends at Goldman Sachs' Marcus platform but scales across our retail, wealth, and corporate banking segments.

Third, robotic process automation and hyperautomation. Deploying UiPath and Automation Anywhere bots enterprise-wide, we've automated 45% of back-office processes, from KYC onboarding to loan origination workflows. This delivered a 25% reduction in non-interest expense growth to 3.2% YoY, versus the street's 5-7% expectation. Productivity per FTE rose 18% to $285,000, driven by reallocating 2,500 roles from routine tasks to high-value advisory services—echoing Wells Fargo's efficiency playbook post their 2020 tech overhaul.

Regionally, these investments are tailored to local dynamics. In North America, which contributes 55% of our tech spend, we've prioritized embedded finance APIs compliant with the CFPB's open banking push, integrating with Plaid and Finicity to capture 15% market share in instant payments. This drove a 22% efficiency gain in our U.S. consumer banking unit. In Europe, amid PSD3 preparations and the ECB's DORA regulations, our €450 million ($490 million) outlay on cybersecurity and ISO 20022 harmonization reduced compliance costs by 19% and positioned us ahead of peers like HSBC. Asia-Pacific, our fastest-growing region at 28% revenue CAGR, saw cloud-native core upgrades in partnership with Temenos Transact, slashing APAC expense-to-revenue by 14 points to 48%, fueled by digital adoption in India and Southeast Asia where mobile banking penetration hit 72%.

Strategically, these investments aren't just cost cutters—they're revenue enablers. Our data lakehouse on Snowflake, now ingesting 50 petabytes daily, powers hyper-personalized offerings like dynamic pricing on deposits, yielding a 15 bps NIM lift, and predictive churn models that retained $3.2 billion in assets under management. Looking ahead to FY2025, we're guiding tech capex at $3.1 billion, with 40% earmarked for genAI expansion, including agentic workflows for trade finance that could unlock $500 million in incremental fee income. Risks remain—vendor concentration and cyber threats—but our 99.99% uptime and $2 billion liquidity buffer in our tech escrow mitigate these.

Finally, as we dive into the credit loss provisions and our reserve dynamics, I'll walk you through the rationale behind our $450 million reserve release this quarter—our first meaningful release since the onset of the pandemic—and how this ties into our robust coverage ratios. This reflects not only the resilience of our $850 billion loan portfolio but also disciplined underwriting and proactive portfolio management amid a normalizing macroeconomic environment.

For Q3, we recorded a net provision benefit of $450 million, bringing our full-year 2024 provision expense to $2.1 billion—a 35% decline from 2023's $3.2 billion amid heightened uncertainty from inflation and rate hikes. This release was driven by a combination of improved forward-looking macroeconomic scenarios under our CECL framework, favorable vintage performance in our consumer and small business segments, and net charge-offs stabilizing at 45 basis points annualized, down from 62 bps in Q3 2023.

Our reserve decisions are anchored in our sophisticated CECL model, which incorporates over 50 macroeconomic variables across base, adverse, and stressed scenarios, weighted 60/25/15 respectively this quarter—up from 50/30/20 last year as tail risks receded. Key drivers included macroeconomic normalization: The FOMC's pivot toward rate cuts, with the fed funds rate peaking at 5.25-5.50% and now projected to ease to 4.00-4.25% by mid-2025 per our internal forecasts, materially lowered our probability of default projections. GDP growth forecasts improved to 2.1% for 2025 from 1.4% six months ago, while unemployment stabilized at 3.8%. This shaved 15-20 bps off our portfolio-wide ECL estimates.

Portfolio-specific performance: Delinquency rates across our book fell 25 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 1.15%, the lowest since pre-COVID levels. In consumer lending—29% of our portfolio, dominated by our flagship PrimeVisa credit cards and auto loans—30+ day delinquencies dropped to 2.1% from 2.6%, reflecting strong wage growth in service sectors and our 15% penetration of Buy Now, Pay Later integrations with partners like Affirm. Charge-offs here moderated to 2.8%, supported by our AI-driven early warning system, which flagged 12% more at-risk accounts via alternative data from Plaid and Experian.

Commercial and CRE caution: We did build $200 million selectively in commercial real estate, where office exposure sits at $18 billion or 2.1% of loans—below peers like Wells Fargo at 3.5%. Rationale? Regional office vacancy rates hit 20% in gateway markets like San Francisco and New York, per CBRE data, prompting a 10 bps PD uplift in our multifamily and office sub-segments. However, this was more than offset by releases in C&I, where investment-grade lines to tech and healthcare drew down 8% amid M&A slowdowns. Comparatively, this positions us favorably versus JPMorgan's $1.2 billion Q3 build, which was CRE-heavy, and aligns with Bank of America's release trajectory as consumer metrics stabilized.

Post-release, our Allowance for Credit Losses stands at $14.8 billion, or 1.74% of total loans held for investment—up 5 bps quarter-over-quarter and 22 bps year-over-year, providing a healthy buffer. Critically, our criticized and classified loan coverage remains elite at 285%, covering 100% of non-performing loans at $2.1 billion, or 0.25% of loans, down from 0.42%.

Segmentally, in consumer: loans $247 billion, ACL $4.2 billion, coverage 1.70%, QoQ delinq change negative 30 bps, NCO rate annualized 2.8%. Commercial: loans $425 billion, ACL $7.1 billion, coverage 1.67%, delinq change negative 15 bps, NCO 0.35%. CRE: loans $85 billion, ACL $2.0 billion, coverage 2.35%, delinq plus 10 bps, NCO 0.55%. International: loans $93 billion, ACL $1.5 billion, coverage 1.61%, delinq negative 20 bps, NCO 0.42%. Total: $850 billion loans, $14.8 billion ACL, 1.74% coverage, delinq negative 25 bps, NCO 0.45%.

Regionally, U.S., 82% of portfolio: pristine performance, with coverage at 1.80% versus the industry average of 1.55% per FDIC data. Our Southeast franchise, bolstered by $10 billion in SBA 7(a) loans, saw zero migration to special mention. Europe, 10%: released $150 million as ECB rates topped out at 4.50%, easing pressure on our €15 billion investment banking-related lines. However, we're monitoring German industrials closely amid 1.2% Eurozone GDP growth. Asia-Pacific, 8%: selective build in China exposure, $4 billion mostly supply chain finance, where property sector woes persist—PDs up 5 bps—but offset by India growth via our HDFC Bank partnership, where digital MSME loans grew 22% with sub-1% delinquencies.

We've invested $75 million this year to enhance our ECL engine, integrating machine learning models from our QuantRisk platform—now processing 10 terabytes of real-time data daily, including satellite imagery for CRE valuations and social sentiment for consumer PDs. This reduced model uncertainty by 18%, per internal back-testing against 2020 stress.

Strategically, we're optimizing via credit migration management: derisking high-LGD office CRE by 15% through non-accrual sales and extending only to trophy assets with 95%+ occupancy. We're also leaning into resilient sectors—healthcare C&I up 12% to $50 billion—and expanding our $30 billion green loan book, which boasts 0.8% coverage on 1.2x collateralized assets.

Looking forward, we expect provisions of $1.8-2.2 billion for 2025, assuming no recession, with coverage ticking up to 1.80-1.85% as we grow loans 4-6%. This discipline underscores our fortress balance sheet—CET1 at 12.8%—positioning Sterling Bank Group to outperform in any cycle.

We are pleased with the progress we are making on our strategic initiatives, and we remain confident in our ability to deliver sustainable value for our shareholders.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator:
Ladies and gentlemen, as a reminder, that is [dial-in] if you'd like to ask a question. Our first question comes from David Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

David Smith:
Good morning. Can you provide some color on the macroeconomic outlook and its impact on loan growth going forward?

John Reynolds:
Good morning, David. Thanks for the question. As Michael outlined, we're navigating a resilient but bifurcated macro with U.S. soft landing intact, supporting 5-7% loan growth in FY25, focused on C&I, resilient CRE like multifamily, and high-growth areas like India's SME digital lending. We've tightened office exposure and hedged China risks, so we're positioned for steady expansion even if unemployment edges higher. Our tech-enhanced underwriting keeps us selective.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Johnson with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Johnson:
Good morning. What is your outlook for operating expenses and efficiency ratio trajectory?

Michael Chen:
Good morning, Emily. We're guiding full-year op ex growth at 3.5-4.5%, with ongoing "Fit for Growth" savings offsetting tech and talent investments. Efficiency ratio heading to 55% by 2026, driven by revenue leverage from fees and embedded finance, plus genAI productivity gains like 30% Tier 1 inquiry automation. Peers are lagging, so we see continued outperformance.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Robert Lee with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Robert Lee:
Good morning. Can you discuss the impact of recent regulatory changes on your loan portfolio and reserves?

Lisa Patel:
Good morning, Robert. Regulatory shifts like Basel III endgame and CECL refinements are embedded in our models, with CET1 at 12.8% providing ample buffer. We've proactively de-risked CRE criticized loans to 2.8%, far below peers, and our $450 million release reflects improved PDs from macro normalization and AI early warnings. Coverage at 1.74% total, 285% on criticized—strong across segments, even with selective CRE builds for office stress. We're compliant ahead on IRRBB and DORA, minimizing portfolio impacts.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn the conference back over to John Reynolds for any closing remarks.

John Reynolds:
Thank you for your interest in Sterling Bank Group. We appreciate you joining us today. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
aspects: Operating expenses: trends and key drivers
Technology investments and their impact on efficiency
Reserve build/release: rationale and coverage ratios

aspect_summary.Macroeconomic outlook and impact: Resilient yet bifurcated global macro with US soft landing (GDP growth 2.1% forecast 2025, unemployment 4.1%, core PCE 2.7%), cooling inflation (global CPI 5.8%), but rising credit card delinquencies (3.2%) and CRE office vacancies (19.5%); supports NIM expansion to 3.45% (+12bps QoQ), tepid 4.2% YoY loan growth (tightened office to 15% portfolio), regional divergence (Europe 0.9%, India 6.8%); guiding 5-7% FY25 loan growth in C&I, resilient CRE, India SMEs.
aspect_summary.Operating expenses: trends and key drive: Adjusted op ex $2.85B, +4.2% YoY/+1.8% QoQ (2.8% ex-$150M one-time mortgage charge); efficiency ratio 57.8% (from 60.2% YoY); personnel +3.1% ($1.48B, merit offset by 4% headcount cut/RPA), tech +12% ($627M, cloud/AI), prof fees +8%, compliance +6%, occupancy flat, marketing -2%; drivers: inflation, talent competition, 'Fit for Growth' $320M savings; FY guide 3.5-4.5% growth, efficiency to 55% by 2026.
aspect_summary.Technology investments and their impact: $2.8B FY24 tech spend (12% op ex, +15% YoY), improving efficiency ratio to 52.3% from 58.1%; cloud 85% migrated (28% TCO cut, STP 98.5%), AI/ML $650M (fraud -42%, call center -32%/$120M savings), RPA 45% back-office automated (productivity +18%/FTE); revenue enablers (15bps NIM lift, $3.2B AUM retention); FY25 guide $3.1B.
aspect_summary.Reserve build/release: rationale and cov: $450M reserve release (first since pandemic, FY24 provisions $2.1B/-35% YoY) driven by improved CECL macro (rate cuts to 4.00-4.25%, GDP 2.1%), delinq -25bps to 1.15%, NCO 45bps; selective $200M CRE office build offset; ACL $14.8B/1.74% coverage (+5bps QoQ/+22bps YoY), 285% criticized/classified, 100% NPLs (0.25%); FY25 provisions $1.8-2.2B, coverage 1.80-1.85%.
